senses.gloss:
Śavarta is the name of a species of ‘worm’ in the Atharvaveda and the taittirīya Saṃhitā.
Foot notes ix. 4, 16, with the various reading Svavarta, Whitney, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 531.
v. 7, 23, 1.
Cf. Zimmer, Altindisches Leben, 98. Possibly Roth is right in holding that the word = śava-varta, a worm ‘living on carrion.’

Śavas is the name of a teacher, a pupil of agnibhū kāśyapa in the vaṃśa brāhmaṇa.
Foot notes Indische Studien, 4, 373.
Śavasa occurs only in the false reading śavasa-Uśinareṣu in the Gopatha brāhmaṇa (i, 2, 9) for sa-Vaśośīnareṣu. See vaśa.

Śaviṣṭha is, according to Ludwig, the name of a generous patron in the Rigveda.
Foot notes Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 163.
viii. 74, 14, 15.

Sāvasāyana, ‘descendant of śavas,’ is the patronymic of Devataras in the vaṃśa brāhmaṇa.
Foot notes Indische Studien, 4, 373.

Savya-ṣṭhā, savya-ṣṭhṛ, Savye-ṣṭha, and savya-stha are all various forms of the word for ‘car-fighter,’ as opposed to sārathi, ‘charioteer,’ showing that, as was natural, the fighter stood on the left of the driver. The commentators are inclined to see in the savyaṣṭhā merely another ‘charioteer,’ but this is quite unjustifiable, and is perhaps due to later caste prejudice against a śūdra charioteer.
Foot notes Av. viii. 8, 23.
Satapatha brāhmaṇa, v. 2, 4, 9; 3, 1, 8; 4, 3, 17, 18.
taittirīya brāhmaṇa. i. 7, 9, 1.
kāṇva recension of the Śatapatha brāhmaṇa, Eggeling, Sacred Books of the East, 41, 62, n. 1; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iv. 3, 8.
On Śatapatha brāhmaṇa, v. 3, 1, 8; taittirīya brāhmaṇa, loc. cit.
Eggeling, loc. cit.; Hopkins, Journal of the American Oriental Society, 13, 235.
Cf. Zimmer, Altindisches Leben, 296.
Sāvayasa (‘descendant of Savayasa’) is the patronymic of Aṣāḍha, or Āṣāḍha, in the Śatapatha brāhmaṇa (i. 1, 1, 7).
